entries.text: Tape 5-A. Interview with Jerry Phillips and David Gould by Bob Zybach, with Amber Ross and Randy Wiest while touring the Elliott State Forest on November 8, 2017. Part 1. The Big Burn to Bear Wallow (47:38}
Haynes Inlet. 0:04 The Big Burn to Bert’s Cabin Photos. No Photos.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: They [Larson family] were here when the 1868 fire was in here. Then built this barn from the timber on what was left over later. They cleaned all this bottom up. Used to be skunk cabbage and willows and stuff. Put hogs out there to eat the stuff [and then channeled the drainage].

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: But I have a recording taken by [Dennis] Signalness and some of the [John and Maralee] Brelage boys -- and the Brelages bought the ranch from [Herman] Larson's. So they took the recording and said the fire of 1868 and talked about it and said it started in Scottsburg [meant Scholfield Creek], which I don't know if that's true.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think it's [Scottsburg] true. That's the facts.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah. Starting in Scottsburg. Or Scholfield Creek, I think.

That would have been people in here and where the terraces are back there. Do you know anything about artifacts or things of that nature?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I don't. They talked about it some, and they were just mainly making a living. Started out that way.

entries.text: Wow. So even with the alder and the salmonberry here, before then it was just a field?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Well they grew potatoes in this part, they had to clean it up a little bit. They had fern like these here, and they had to get rid of the logs. Plowing it up -- he had a plow -- and then they found a scraper tool they used, and the kids would throw them [potatoes] up over the bank.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: These alder here, did they grow up after the potato patch then?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Oh yeah that's all grown up since then. This wasn't here at one point, just snags.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So we're on the old Elkhorn homestead right now basically?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Just about, yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, so the potato patch was . . .

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Down here, yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, just a little bit off the land claim.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: You got to realize the whole forest down here was to build a ranch. To run cattle on it was the main aim, to get the cattle range on the whole watershed.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But when they made the claim on the land it didn't include this necessarily.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: No. I think they got the timber sale over there now. The Elkhorn Ranch timber sale was logged. Protestors tried to stop it, but we ran them off so they got to logging.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We got that covered in, that story is in your [SWOCC student] report [Big Fires, The Elkhorn Ranch, and the Elliott State Forest, 2013].

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I visited those same people that was in the Elkhorn, in the valley here a couple weeks ago.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Was it the same group or the exact same people?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Well the same group . . . Forest Service was there; they didn't do anything.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Jerry the whole time you were managing this was there any protests at all ever on any of the logging sales or anything?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No, there were some complaints, very minor ones about aerial spraying.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah-hah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I made it a point to go out personally and talk to all those neighbors every time. Tell them when we were going to do it, ask where their water source was, and happy them up, and we didn't have any major problems. We've got accommodations from our state office on avoiding that. Because of course, every forest has people that live around the edge.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So any conflicts are mostly just neighboring landowners, there weren't any organizations or anything like that?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No, nope. We didn’t have any problems like that.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: We're on the Elkhorn Ranch property, here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So was this all cleared?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah this was cleared and the grass was all on it. The old maid, Oela, and my great grandmother was out here with a cross-cut saw cutting up logs to get wood once in a while.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Now in the summer there's campers in here all the time.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: You got the people with four wheelers who just love to come in here and tear it up, too.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: We had trouble with that on the other side. They want to tear up my grass and we didn't like it, but I've got them trained now.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It was a popular place for the hippies back in the ‘70s.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah the “Elkhorn Express” [music group] got their name from out here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right -- music group; their name for it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Which “butte” [misunderstood name]?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This place.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Music group.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Elkhorn Express.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: There's the waterfall there, see it?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, so it's just more of a ripple.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah, that's where they have the hole, that's where the kids would come swim and stuff. I brought Chief Brainard of Coos out here and told him about the stories of the Indian families that were in here when the fire went through, got in the water, and one of the daughters died there it got so hot.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So that's right at this spot here? And where'd you hear that story from?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I heard that from my grandparents, about the Indians.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's where the trail comes down there from the ridge.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So when we turned off way back there that would have connected up to here [2000, 2300, and 2320]?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah that connects here yeah, I opened that up a bit last year. So you could find it and people can walk it if they want.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So it would be the trailhead basically, the story was that the Indians were here in the 1868 fire and a little girl drowned in that spot? Wow.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: So that's the ranch there?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The last of the apple trees are still bearing apples.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But it's on the other side of the river?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: We can go over there if we keep going. I'm pretty sure we can get across.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Oh, and of course there were lots of apple trees there. We want pictures? My book shows how many.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Is that the apple trees over there?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, good.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The bears are raised up on apple trees.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Beavers raise heck with them, too. They were cutting them down. We had to put wire around them. I got up here too late and they had to cut a bunch of them down.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: One of the orchards that I documented on a school forest went back to the late 1840s and about two years later half of them were wiped out by beaver.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: There's no gravel at all in there [West Fork Millicoma], if you look at it. No sand either.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's why they keep dredging Coos Bay.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah. That's one of the loads of silt that come in to Coos Bay after the 1868 Fire.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Exactly.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That's what the old-timers talked about. They run around out there in boats and knew when it was coming in, too.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well that looks like a plantation over there now.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: My daddy cleaned that off in the ‘60s. It had been thinned, they plowed it until the end of the field, right there. And this side creek comes in here; we called this Shake Creek. That's where we got a lot of shingles from, right here. This stream here is another slide come in, this all slid in there. Some of them come off the ridges up at the 2000 clear down here. Took the culvert out, and you can see the big rocks out in the river, and that would have been six feet high in the river there at one point.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Washed out here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Is the island still in Gould Lake?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah it's there, but it isn't an island. You can see the rock. I've been down on the rock. This is about the other end of the property, 160 acres.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So we've been in it up through that whole draw back there?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Oh yeah, just a little ways past the potato patch. We got to turn right up here somewhere.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Do you see a place to turn around, Randy?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: We can go across the river I think, and go to the other side.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Oh we can go across the river?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Is that it there, Jerry?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That looks like it. Yeah that's it there.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: You turn here?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Now we've been passing some alder trees. Do those go back to when your grandparents were there or great grandparents?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: This whole thing was burned off in 1868.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right. You see that in that picture.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The [old 1880-1890] pictures show you that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay but I mean these trees here then were allowed to come in or did they come in after . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: These all came in after ‘68.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, but not after the Goulds left?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No, no.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay so these were growing while the Goulds were here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They left about 1914.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Well the field was pretty well cleared. There was just a few openings when I it opened back up. If you look over there you see the alder stubs and how open that is? So I'm saying the alder die and then you get that, see? See what I'm saying? You got the opening there and it’s all brush.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Then you see one of the big snags up there.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yep. Are we actually gonna cross the creek?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I think so, let me go down and see how deep it is.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yeah, that'd be a good idea.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I'm sure it’ll be okay.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So there's no road into the old homestead? You got to cross the river here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: People used to cross it lower down. But they sold a little bit of timber over here, just a small amount of timber, a little thinning sale, and we put in a concrete crossing.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, so there's an actual crossing built in to here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: See that? Glae was willing to sell the place, the whole place, to a private buyer, but he demanded that they promise to never do any harvesting.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well of course no one would agree to that, so then I managed to persuade him he should trade it to me, and we would trade some wood around there. We always had some good wood to trade. That's one of the assets we had - - we had about 5000 acres of scattered Common School lands, just out everywhere. So I could always offer one of those to whoever the interested people were. We always found a taker to those trades, so this was traded to International Paper, and then they traded it to us except for five acres, because they wanted to keep five acres. That's what they still have.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But this is the only way into the five acres?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yep. Yeah, it is. To the part they still own.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Does it look like we can make it?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Are we doing it?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yep, you betcha. I mean why not? We've come this far right?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah we got this far. What's it like on the other side though?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: It's good.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Gravel?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I put gravel on last time I was here, actually. It's all solid concrete along bedrock. There is a bump right in the middle of this here, right about there.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Hang on to your hat, just in case.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I went across there with my daughter. Coming back out we went sideways about eight inches. Scared the piss out of me.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's right you can't swim.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Oh I can swim now, but I mean just not that summer.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Might not be anymore apples in the apple trees.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I was hoping to get a picture of one. I can at least get the tree.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: There might be some up . . . but they’re pretty high, is the trouble.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: This is cool. I haven't been over here.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: See they had fields way up where we're at and they had a ditch down through here that went to the mill with water. When we get further down you can see where the ditch was, they cut the road on it. See this is all growing back since the ‘60s when my dad was in here to clean it up.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The fir?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah, fir, alder, and everything else. This was all bare out until the edge of the river. Planted it back into grass.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: He was a man who was full of ideas. He was gonna rebuild the old house.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: There wasn't any old house to rebuild.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Dave is a good son. Also full of ideas.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But you're not gonna rebuild the house are you?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: No. I had to watch my dad fighting with people and I knew it didn’t work very good. I don't mean fight, I mean just argue and sometimes lose. Got the battle of the Trust Land now, and I can't get much headway. Jim Paul knows what I think, there's no doubt about that.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Here's one apple tree right here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Some right there.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: There’s a little bit of land that they built on there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Where's the rose bush at?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: It's right behind us.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh okay.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Continue on?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: We can go on across and we'll turn around up ahead and come back if you want.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It'd be good to get oriented where the house is and everything. A lot of silt built up on there. Looks like somebody's got a water line in there?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: They'll be down here in the summertime so I can build a fire in here, is what I do. Just enough water I can do that. It's going a long way up the hill, here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Up the hill?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: We're going to show you where the logging was.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We're still on the five acres.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow. So the five acres, does that include water rights?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yes. The water comes out right there. It's on the property.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It starts on the river and comes this way.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Probably going to have to turn around not too far past where we're at.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay. Continue on or stop?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: We're just a little bit more. This is pretty good spot here.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Good here?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah, the corner of the property’s right over there, and the other corner’s right down just by the water at the bottom on the left side over here, and comes back to the river.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: So Randy, up on one of the hills above us, in that clearcut is where the protesters chained themselves to the trees.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Oh right up here?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I want to get a couple pictures here.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Want to get out for a picture, Bob?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, what was here David? Was a house or anything up here? I'm just trying to get oriented.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: There was a building up here. I think it was just for, I don't know what it was for.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, so . . .

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: They actually plowed this up here too. I've got records of that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, so here's the old homestead, there's the barn.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: We're right up here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We're over here. So we drove past it. So where was the orchard in relation to here?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The buildings were in here, and I think over here, too.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, so the orchard's here, and we're on this, is that a road right there? A skid trail? It looks like they've got this all logged off.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: No that's all burnt, that's what it was, they didn't do anything to that. They burnt this off several times while they were in here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Where'd they get the wood for the houses and everything?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Well there was some cedar in the bottom, but most of it was growing on Shake Creek, up here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: He sawed the lumber in the sawmill here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. Well I was just thinking on the picture . . . it’s fairly bare up through here, and I was thinking maybe that's where they got the logs for the sawmill.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: No that was just in the burn. Like this, see it was open, there's no snags in here, this was all open the same thing over there. We’re actually in a stream meander here, you can't really notice the stream went up around here that's why its high right there. A long time ago it was a stream meander. If you looked, there's actually river gravel in this hill up here I've looked at. And you go on up the river and you have a lot of this stream meandering around and big, big bends and they were asking me how come the gradient was so steep. It was hard for the fish to find us and that's the main reason, because of the meander's would break out. When it broke through the meanders, you see them on the maps.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What broke through, like slides?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: No they just broke through here after one took off. I can show you several of them in Elk Creek. There's a good example up there.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Oxbows.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So we're over in here, we're gonna come back down around on the return. Can you tell me when we get near the homesite?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah, we're going right through it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, yeah I wanted to get a reading there and a couple photos. That and the orchard.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Well, they logged this unit here, so it was Elkhorn Ranch original property here. It was a 40-acre piece that went up here -- they actually got a few of them up here -- that’s why they needed access.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: How come they didn't take out some of these bigger trees?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: You mean now? Well they grew back after they were here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: No I mean for the sale.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The sale stopped at the property line out there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, so this is on your five acres then?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah, when they logged this they had a tail-hold tied to two of these big trees behind us. They did it so it didn't kill them, I told them they could go

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: ahead and do it. They run a skyline up through here. This was actually kind of a road up here we didn't have to do too much work to it. My dad wanted to build a house right on the point of the claim in here. It never happened. This belongs to my daughter now. She doesn't know what's going to happen to it either.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: David I think your doors open.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So the five acres is in your daughter’s name now?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah. I see these big trees they grew back after the fire. Those trees are about the same size as a lot of the snags right around here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah I was curious about that on the ages on the diameters.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I've been reading some of that stuff you've got there.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Better angle here.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah that's a hard angle.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That's got some river gravel on it. No point in seeing it today.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well it seems to me on this spawning gravel thing that it keeps washing out.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah, it just goes.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Then what happens to the fish?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Well they’ve got to wait for the next one. Like Jake [Bob Jacobson] was saying, they spawn in the gravel that's up on the sides.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: ‘Cause there's no gravel in the bottom. But they got to do it [spawn] when the water's there; see when there’s the high water, and they got to be done by the time the water goes down. I think he said they need two weeks, I can't remember. We've just come off the beds there with solid rock. The property goes right about 20 feet from us, right out to the river. I wish he would have done it differently, but he did what he wanted to. Now the bridge would have been back over in front of us.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The bridge? Now that's the 70-foot span one?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. I'd like to take a picture of that and then the orchard’s down next isn't it?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: So you want to walk up there?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yes, please. Now this road here, does that lead down to where the bridge was?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The bridge should have been right . . . probably right here somewhere.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. How about that road behind us there, where's that go?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That goes to another crossing we don’t use anymore.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The barn used to be right up here and the road was to put hay in the barn. Look behind us and you can see it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay so this is where the barn was?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah. See that little bench here? That's how we'd eventually get the hay in the barn. Top of the barn.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Up through there?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: What'd you do break something off?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: The little antennae came off.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I’ve got a lot of sentimental value here. Nobody else has. I can't believe that they’re not going to log this thing. Crazy.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's all politics. It's not science.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: It's not history or anything.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No, it’s not even money. It's all politics.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The reason why this is like it is, is because this is kind of like an alluvial fan out here and a little further up it's actually boggy up there. And you dig down in there, it's a lot of gravel in it too. I was telling him the barn was right here and that little bench up there is how they got up to get in the loft of the barn.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Oh is that right?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah they cut hay here and put it in the barn.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: So the foundations and everything are gone?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Everything's gone, yeah.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: It's gone?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Well it was all set on cedar blocks, or it might have been set on a piece of rock or something.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: It was all built on cedar, red cedar, but then after they left the house burned down, people would come and just take pieces of the building part and burn them for firewood.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The house was here until 1945.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Is that right?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Then some hunters got to messing around, they'd built a fire and burnt the house down.

entries.speaker: David Gould

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This part of that same road is on Beaver Creek.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: You got a 4% grade or a 6% grade, or something? You can haul logs on it I know.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think we planned it for seven. It's whatever the roads . . . the trucks were able to run adverse loads on them.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: It needs maintenance here. This bit of the road here, too. [No log hauls so no money for maintenance on the 2300. DGG.]

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We had one of the roads that ran an adverse of nine percent.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Coming out of Elk Creek [9300].

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Now Elk Creek is where the Gould Lake is, isn't it?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It is, it is.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah. We need to go down here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's interesting if . . . 65 years ago it was a nice little lake. Now it's all totally gone.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Is that right? Wow, but filled in with sediment?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, and vegetation. Just it never was deep, and a landslide lake.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Some of the landslide eroded and the water level dropped. The lake also collected sand from the stream above.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, the lake had fish in it, didn't it?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Oh yeah. [After the state started logging the sediment filled it in about 20 years. DGG]

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I think one of those stories -- I wasn't too clear if it was Gould Lake or Loon Lake -- but they caught like 160 fish out of it or something.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That's Gould Lake, there was a lot of fish in there. I never got to go fishing there, either.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We had that happen in Lincoln County where you had the Slide Lake coming in, create a large, about 90-acre slide, created what we called Slide Lake, and then about three years later I took my boat up there and it was just loaded with large fish that quick.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: I recently fished at the head of Slide Lake.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Slide Lake?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yup.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I heard that get formed. That formed the day before Christmas that year. They called it Ayers Lake for a while, after Ray Ayers. They blamed it on the clearcut logging, but what had happened was it was starting to go and they went in there and clearcut to get the trees out before they slid off the hill. And then when the slide went, we were planting trees and the loggers were shut down. We just heard a giant boom, and we were all trying to figure out what happened, and then we found out after vacation when the loggers went back there all their stuff was isolated [on the other side of the slide]. All the trees planted on it, my crews planted it.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Is that right?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That was pretty easy planting.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: I used to hike in there as a kid, high school fishing quite a bit.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I took my boat in there and left it, and then somebody else took it, so.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yeah, I remember there was a boat back in there. We never did use it but I remember seeing a boat back in there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I had a 14-foot aluminum boat.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yeah. We packed a little canoe in there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. We're talking about the same Slide Lake in Lincoln County right?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yup.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. Yup. It sounded like a supersonic jet went right over. It went kaboom, and we were like . . . there was a reverberation and everybody -- it was pretty clear -- we thought somebody had been up there blowing up dynamite or something.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I heard something on the Slide Lake, that something happened, I just didn't know what it was.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The next year.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That was the same with us. In fact, it was the next year when the guys came back from Christmas break.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: This was a big slide area here. It's come down pretty often. I bet Jerry had fun laying the road out [2300 Road switchbacks].

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Did you lay this road out Jerry?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yup.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Did you have fun?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Sure.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: He had to walk in a ways.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What year did this road go in?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We sold the sale in '58, built the mainline road in '59, and then logged it all off in 1960.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Before the Columbus Day Storm even?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yup.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: There’s not a switchback in the whole road.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Big sale. It was like 220 acres, and we had allowed them to cat log it. We would never do that anymore, but we were new to the market. Loggers all knew how to deal with BLM, but we were a new marketer.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We tried to be generous in the conditions of the contract. We wouldn't be . . . we sold it as a scale sale for one thing, not on the cruise. They would log without any confidence, since we were new to cruising.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We sold it with a scaling platform put in out to the road, where it's a state highway. Paid a scaler, had to Cat log most of it.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Spent all your time designing this road over here. Didn't have time for getting there.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The negative thing was that we still had those, still thought we could aerial seed successfully. We got this off-site seed up from Washington.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That was used for this area here too?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right. This area right here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It didn't work out really well. It was poor quality fir seed, from the Quinalt area.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They say Steilacoom, or something.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: This isn't the same sale we came in from the other side on is it?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Same seed, probably.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: We're getting close to the 1000 road.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. Let's make a mark for that.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah, and then we're going to take the 9000 this way.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Everybody was choosing seed by seed zones.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh. One thing I was hoping to see today, unless it's on the west slope, is the progeny test sites.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right. We have three.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We're part of a co-op, and International Paper, and BLM, and ourselves, and there were test sites on all those ownerships.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Then all the . . . actual plantations then went up to St. Paul after the seedlings had grown and the seed bearing progeny trees.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They weren't grown here on the forest?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They were all grown to a seed processing plant. That may have been over in Elkton for the extraction –seed -- then they were all grown up at St. Paul.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I thought there was three test sites on the forest?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: There are.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, so --

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Those are the . . . I guess bigger trees in here. These are some genuine old- growth here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: You're saying old-growth but they go back to --

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: These are . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, there are some big trees.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: . . . go back to 1750.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This is genuine old-growth here. We just left it here just to look at it.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Now, this grew up after the 1840 fire, or what?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The 1840 fire as far as we knew was all in the southeast part of the forest, Cedar Creek and Owl Creek, and Salander Creek. These are all like 1750.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Very fine timber.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: How come this didn't get logged?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We just like to look at it.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: They didn’t want to log it, just keep it to enjoy it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Are we on Jerry's Reserve right here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: No. This is one of the set-asides.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This is the same age, but it's just a small parcel.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Real nice stuff.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: We're kind of close to there. I think it's that square down there [on the GIS map].

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh. Yeah, I know it's that 40 there. We're there where the red dot is?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yup.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow, so that's right along the --

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: -- head of Beaver Creek.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Randy, we're going to pop out on the 1000 for a short distance.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay, go left?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Turn left here.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I didn't realize that there's still another patch of old-growth through here.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: I think you might be above the log trucks.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: But you never know.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: You never know. We'll find out.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah. This is the road we can take to Allegany.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This is one of all the waterholes around here. Do chain checks?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Oh yeah?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah, still some water in it.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yup.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Is that rain or just . . .?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, just a spring.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Wasn't some of this timber in here a little bigger when you were logging?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: 1000 over here?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Here, you want this stuff bigger in here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This half section here is where . . . Board of forestry ownership.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The half sitting right in front of us.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The head of Silver Creek.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Jerry, we just came by a spring there. Can we mark that spring on the map?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Pardon?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: You want me to go back to it?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I think we're close enough.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It's too much trouble really to get out, but I wanted to get the springs marked to kind of get them --

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: I can turn around pretty easily and go back if you want.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, it --

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: The waterholes should be labeled on these maps.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, let's see. One of the maps . . .

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Hey Randy, our truck just sprung a leak.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: It did?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: I'll be darned. It must be . . . yeah, from the new window.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah. If you . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Got this map there. I thought I had it down in there.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: You should. That's my copy.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, yeah. We don't want . . . Let's see.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: There, these are more copies but I highlighted through these. So I don't really see that waterhole there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Here it is.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: That waterhole is not labeled.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, we can just --

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: But I can mark it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, good. There's the map. There's that. Not a very good functioning office space here.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I should have brought my car, and we could have used that, too.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: There we go.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Alright.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Good?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay. That's a big roundabout.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Big Saddle.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I don't see any truck hauling in there.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Big Saddle.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Big Saddle.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Then south section, we logged all of that in 1960. It's all old-growth. Then that's all grown back, then we went to log it again, and then somebody found a bird in there.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah, we're at the 10-Mile [road marker]. We should be good on log trucks.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay. It doesn't look like they've been driving on this.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: It doesn't.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Nope.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Okay. I think they're from the seven and a half mile to the south.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What's this ridgeline called through here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Elk Ridge. Elk Ridge.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: This is Elk Creek down here [9000].

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This is our original main road [1000].

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The West Fork's on this side. The divide is here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What are the two creeks on the . . .?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I don't know. One of them's Beaver Creek and Trout Creek and now Elk Creek is the one we are on now.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: We're going to take the next major left.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Next major left, okay.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Do you see all this shale in the bank here?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Could be a gate on it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yup.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That's on top of the sandstone. That's what makes the loose spawning gravel on it that comes off here and goes on down to the river.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So it's the shale that's forming the spawning gravel, not the sandstone?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: No, It's the sandstone from the slides.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yup, this is our major left.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This is Elk Creek. We're down Elk Creek.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Now we're heading over into the Elk Creek drainage right at this point?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah, this is it.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: On the 9000 Road.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: How come the gate's back there? When they're logging or something they lock them up?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: No, that was from the protestors. All of the interior of the forest was gated out.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: They put one down there at Elkhorn, where you go into the Elkhorn. They had them waiting on them when they did that. The judge said they couldn’t go in there or hang around, so they put in gates to keep them out. Spent a lot of money and it just went down the drain. [They put gates in to restrict protester access to the logging sites. A judge said it was against the law to exclude the public, so the state could not lock the gates. DGG]

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah, so this is the 2000 where we started.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah-ha.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: This is the 1000. Any of these interior drainages were all gated, so that's where the protestors were.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Is that when the signs came down too, with the protestors here, or was that . . .?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: No, the signs came down because we have no longer a managed forest.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: All this timber on the left . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Another deer.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Another one, that's almost the one we saw earlier.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah, he might have just hopped up the hill.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yeah, wherever.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: This one looked a little bit larger. Of course, my eyesight's going so . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: All this timber on the left, all along here we thought was so nice looking we didn't want to cut it. We just wanted to look at it.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Straight trees!

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's now about 130, 140 years old. Very high quality.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Would you sell it today?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Probably, yes.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It's worth a whole lot more.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: According to the environmentalists.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, they'd say it's worth so much you can't afford to cut it.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Almost certainly it's full of birds.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: When you leave the trees, you leave the habitat.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: People would just walk in from Allegany up and down this ridge to go fishing in Gould Lake.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right. People say they lived in, on Glenn Creek over there. They'd walk over this trail.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: They'd come right down on this ridge here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: A good trail.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: It's not bad. My dad brought my grandmother, or my mother, up here when they was dating. Took her fishing. She kept getting behind and she would come up over the hill to Silver Falls, climbing on the tree, she's getting behind. He'd just say, "Oh the bear's getting closer" boy, she would take off. That wore her out I guess.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: She married him anyhow?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: She told me about that later.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: There's trees out there but they're a little bit bigger.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, that looks like a lot of the snags that we're going through. It's like two basic age classes with an older story and then the second-growth underneath. Is that Doug fir, hemlock, combination mostly?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's 1840 stuff.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: If it has hemlock in it, it's probably that 1840 then.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The other area didn't have hemlock, did it?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Which means that there was still a hemlock seed source available when this was open, and later there wasn’t any hemlock seed source.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And earlier there wasn't any hemlock seed source -- if the 1750 trees didn't have any hemlock in them.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well, it's hard to tell with those. Hemlock doesn't live quite as long.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: According to the Weyerhaeuser specs, very few of these trees ever make it to 400 years. What do you think on hemlock? 200, 250 maybe?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think somewhere in there. I saw some true old-growth hemlock one time, Mount Rainier, and it is quite interesting to look at. The bark looks quite different.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I saw a couple of them, too, on Kentuck.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Hemlock?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah. They were with the old-growth above the mill pond.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: About four-foot on the butt.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I saw the picture of you and your grandfather with that one old-growth.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That's real old-growth there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That looks like maybe eight-foot diameter.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: No, it was bigger than that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: 10 foot?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah. Somewhere around there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I wouldn't say how old they were.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That must go back to what . . . Lionel Youst was saying that went back to the 1400s.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I don’t know

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I don't either. I don't know where he got that number.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I want to know . . . To the left, isn't it?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yup.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The other road goes up into upper Elk Creek and that's where they were running cattle.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: When they came in here originally the trees were much smaller. The trees would protect the elk from the snow. That's where you get your 1840 fire. But those trees were small trees here, but they weren't out in the open.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Just along the perimeter?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Just along this 1840 perimeter. What I keep saying is the 1840 fire is where it was coming across the Umpqua from Scottsburg. This is the edge of it here. The 1868 fire started going from Loon Lake and then southward, maybe some over by Scholfield. I'm not sure about that. I don't see the lake right there. You can see it on maps and everything real plain. It will say right on the map, the fire is coming through to here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I'd be interested in seeing it and also interested in looking it up in the other survey notes around the perimeter, but Jerry you think the fire started in Scottsburg in 1868?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right. See, that's what the people said who were immigrating here, coming to Scottsburg, coming down the river. It was those folks in '68, they're the ones who said that. It was burning on both sides of the river, going southeast, going clear to the Lakeside.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Now this . . . I think really it is a very complex fire history. The whole thing, and then no one really knows exactly how it is. People have ideas and stories, but I think no one is really sure about that. It must have been half a dozen fires in that time period. The only one that CTA said, well I know is confirmed by pioneer settlers.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The 1840 fire, when David was at my house, I was looking for a book that I had in which a couple missionaries come across in 1840. entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: To them.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.text: It's a pretty good patch over there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Second-growth, and you keep going down until you got the third-growth. The third-growth was smaller by like this [showing with arms].

entries.text: And very little defects. Very little defects, whereas true old-growth has quite a bit of defects.
