entries.text: We'll come back around this way here. This road goes to Huckleberry Ridge there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh that's Huckleberry Ridge? Do you call it Huckleberry Ridge or Joe's Ridge?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Joe's Ridge, that's what it is. Blackberries or whatever . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Black huckleberries is what some people call those evergreens.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah, I don't. My grandparents used to put them in sugar and barrel them; layer of sugar and put them in barrels and they'd cure by the end of the wintertime. I saw a fox here one day.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well when I saw you the other day we saw an eagle, and then you said you saw an eagle down here. How often have you seen those?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Well they come in when the salmon are up here at the time. They come in here, not too many of them for the past few years.
Stop #B-35. 16:46 CCC Road to “Dean’s Mountain.” Photos (4): 0989; 0990; 0991; 0992.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Part of the CCC route, here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So this is the CCC road up to Dean’s Mountain?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It is.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: It doesn't look too much different when my grandparents brought me out here. Except it's got rock on it, it didn't have rock then.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: They're filling [forested] holes. See how much opening you get in these groves? Guess that's what those birds need to land in.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It still amazes me, when they built their camps, they swore they were not going to lose a single day's work, ever. And they didn't. They carried that out for seven years. They never lost a day's work, and they took Sunday off. And they never killed a man. Here are all these 18, 19 year-old boys,

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: no hard hats, no canopies for the tractors, using explosives all the time, never killed a single kid.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: They got a lot done, too. It’s not a very big camp where we’re going.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They broke all of today's industrial accident rules.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That's why they're still alive, I guess.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: They focused on staying safe instead of being protected?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well I went around and interviewed three of them for my book, and I found all those three.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Kids from the city, too, they got some of them.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Scattered all around western Oregon, and Charleston, Brownsville, all these different places. Of course some went back home again. Some were from Missouri.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Jerry, if you had to do it over, would you still have them convert the myrtle to fir, or would you tend to just leave the myrtle as it is?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well, we have so little of it that that was never really a question that we dealt with. We probably would have left it, since there's so little, but the mission was, originally, to try to grow pure Douglas fir on all the land that was available. Of course, you had to try to harvest all the old-growth fir, get rid of it, ‘cause it wasn't growing, and get rid of all the alder, ‘cause it was worthless, and then get pure Douglas fir in all the rest. So you would eliminate maple -- of course, we had very little maple -- and myrtle, which was also very, very little. But we're living in this day and age where we're celebrating diversity of all kinds, so we probably would've been directed at an HCP [ESA Habitat Conservation Plan] to keep it.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: You all want to go down to the waterhole first?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Sure, and we got to come back this way too, don't we?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: ‘Cause the waterhole's down that way and the lookout's down that way.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well, you want to turn right here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We'll get it on the way back.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: You intend to go up to Deans Mountain?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I don't know if we can get up there or not, but we can see the road from here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Probably a locked gate.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah, we've got a key, we can get up there.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I haven't been up there for. . .well, I guess it's been forty years. And I know it's changed totally, but it's still there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well that's one of the most historic places on the whole forest.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's the most historic. I said in my book –

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: It’s clearcut now.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What's that?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: It's clear cut now.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's probably the only. . .

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: We're here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: . . . it's the only landmark most people know on the forest.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Oh yeah, it's hard left.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Right, right up there? Okay, I gotcha.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I didn't realize the gate . . .

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Can we turn around?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Not much we can do with all this fog.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I'll tell you a funny story, I just got engaged to Donna down there when we were camped out.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: There's going to be a gate.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Right there.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah, we camped out down there, and I come up here to check the lookout out, and some gal is on the lookout up there, and she talked to me a little bit, wanting me to stay the night, watch the sun come up, and I said "I don't think so."

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I don't think your girlfriend would like it.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Should be locked.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I guess on that little device . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: She must've been lonesome.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Is that thing on?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yup.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Oh. [Recorder turned off until Dean Mountain gate unlocked]

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: . . . story he didn't want recorded.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Oh! [laughter]

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: . . . you know, for the State Forester, it had become a place for relaxation and fun. So there was a knotty pine cabin. And the CC’s meant to build the Benson Ridge Road clear back to where we are now, and up to here. But that never happened.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: You've got that story pretty well explained in your book.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think so.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: One thing, the museum's now got the copy of the PDF file, but your book should be rescanned, because they did it a while back when they didn't have such good software, and it's got a lot of glitches in it. Not real disconcerting, but real obvious, so it could be fixed.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well that's important.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: This is it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, need to take a photo or two here.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: So, we can. . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Fog, fog, fog.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: On the other side of this fence, there's a foundation.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Perfect.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: I'm going to get out of here somehow.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: On a good day, you can see everywhere here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Our radio shop always liked this place. They liked to come out here.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: It would break down, they'd come up and work on it, huh? Have to try this cookie after all.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I wonder why they'd log this here, so they could have better view for the tower?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: They did that down at the other tower down there, too.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, Cougar Pass. Trail Butte. All of them.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: You just don't see the big stumps up in this country.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: There were some, but not as many.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I probably already told you that. Over on Knife Ridge, that was a very good stand of high-quality fir, but when they got through Elkside's [Lumber Co.] fallers claimed more pay for counting all the snags than they did for the green timber. Because there was so many. And now they're all gone, they've all fallen down.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Environmental people want all those snags so they can get them back into the soil I guess. Trouble is, that'll burn and put all that crap in the air up first.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well I didn't have to take any panoramas.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: You could've taken one and duplicated it.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I might actually have the original panoramas.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What's that?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I might actually have the original panoramas here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I've got access to most of them, I've got 35 or 40, including Chetco Peak. I got them online, on the internet.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Really!

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Could you stick your head out there and see?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah, if you swing right. . .

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: I don't want to hit that foundation though.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It's been kind of a hobby of mine to go around to all the old lookouts and take the modern pictures and then get the older pictures. They were throwing away a bunch of them in Siuslaw National Forest when I was going to school at Oregon State and Bill Atkinson gave me permission to gather them up and put them on a camera stand and take a bunch of 35 mm slides of them.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Good!

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They should have those in the archives at OSU.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They should be of value there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. And then there's a group called “I Am Who” that put a bunch of the old 30's Osbourne photos online. And they were doing the same thing I was doing, except they were a lot better funded I think. They got most of them in Oregon and Washington.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Doesn’t take these small stumps long to rot, does it? They disappear pretty fast.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This was staffed during World War II as an aircraft warning station.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Was this the only one in the Elliott? Wasn't there another one? Was it Elk Peak or something that also had a World War II [lookout station]?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It wasn't Elk Peak, that hasn't been used since about 1920. Well, I think Blue Ridge might've been.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah-hah. It seems to me like there was two of them.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Blue Ridge would be radio.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Wasn't there a tower just for TVs or something?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Japanese. World War II. They were constant lookout for incoming aircraft.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: See, Trail Butte was built in 1940.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So that would've been for World War II. That was the other one, wasn't it? Trail Butte and Dean's Mountain. I think that's right.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: It's still raining out.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Thank you. Good thing!

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: You people from Bend probably don't like the rain.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: We both grew up in the [Willamette] Valley.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: We grew up in the Valley. You get to the point doing Christmas trees, you didn't even bother wearing rain gear.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. Well that's why I couldn't stand to wear rain gear for all the years I worked in the woods, ‘cause I would just sweat so much I'd be sopping wet.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And smell bad, just . . . rain is just more comfortable.
Stop #B-36. 29:58 Umpcoos Road to Mud Flat Side Camp. Photos (7): 0993; 0994; 0995; 0996; 0997; 0998; 0999

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: You want to turn left here, in order to get to Muddy Springs.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Turn left? Okay.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Now this is the same water source they used for Dean Mountain lookout?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They, at least, part of the time . . . they also . . . there was a water drip over rock bluff on the other side, they might've used that a while, too.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It's interesting, usually in oral histories I've done in the past you go out and do all this and then do all the background, but with these guys having major books, I'm more familiar with the history of this and them before we even headed out. It's kind of a . . .

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Luxury.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. It's more interesting.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: So, this is all CC construction here too.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Put this on the map here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We relocated only a few hundred feet. Of all their 28 miles of roads. Their location was so good.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They put all the old 3-C buildings on national registers, or most of them, I don't know about the one like at Waldport and stuff like that, but they got most of them registered anymore. A lot of their rock work, but I don't think they've included their road networks. And to me that seems like one of their major accomplishments.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It was. Phone lines were important too, because they were all the old boundary lines, so they've been abandoned.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, but look at it, we're still driving the same road these kids built 70, 80 years ago. No -- 80 or 90 years ago. And it's still working fine.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's Dean's Ridge. We'll just turn to the right here.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Turn to the right? Okay.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: This is the Umpqua over here, and the Elkhorn is there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The Umpcoos Road. We came into this further down, didn't we? It seems like we were on it before.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: I think so.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The CC’s did a lot of work here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Do they still call it the Umpcoos, or does it have a different name?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: That's Umpcoos Ridge, it's the 7000 Road.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Everybody who's worked here calls it that.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I think they should call it the Brown Feather Road or something.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Are murrelets brown, or owls?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I had a picture of them [a murrelet egg] -- it looked just like the ground. Well, they nest on the ground, too.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, mostly.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Most started by nesting on the ground. Just happens to be that they got in the trees down here so they can stop logging, isn't it?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I don't know how many they've found in trees, it's not very many. I remember the first one was a big deal, and I haven't heard of too many since then.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This is the Muddy Springs right here.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That's why they're endangered, they can't find . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The camp was just on the upper side of the road here. And then the spring's over here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Is that the spring right there?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: You can't quite see it yet.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: You can pull up.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: You want me to pull up?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Then we're on the ridgeline again.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's the spring right there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, oh that was. Wow.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: It's a waterhole now.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: It's a waterhole now.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's a waterhole.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I need a picture.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: You want to --

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, please.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It changed into a helicopter waterhole.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Was that always a big spring like that?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well, yeah, it's been, it had a bigger dam around the edge, but that's what it's always been.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: How deep is that?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Oh, maybe six feet.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Six feet?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Bit tight for a helicopter. Take water out of there you think. Think they would've cut more of the trees around there. . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: And of course you didn't have any good rocks to use, so I'm sure it was named Muddy Springs for a good reason. Everything around here, if they walked or drove around here, they were in mud.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That stuff gets pretty slick too.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I was going to tell you, on the other hillside across there, you used to see a albino elk over there, a cow. Only time I've ever seen an albino animal. But it was pretty much pure white. A little bit kind of cream colored. I don't know if somebody shot it or what.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: So this square mile right in front of us here is another piece of State Board of Forestry timberland. In fact, I am inclined to think it's the first piece of land they ever owned.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: This piece here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They acquired this in 1936, from Douglas County, as a tax delinquent piece of ground. It was a very good piece, very good timberland.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: It's got good soil on it. More clay. Makes a pretty good waterhole, huh?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well this is pretty impressive how these are all lining up like this, the ridgeline trails with the springs with the . . .

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Are we turning around from here?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What was that spring like before they turned it into a waterhole?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well it was shallower. But ever since the CC's were here, it's been a place you could get water. Just it was – they’ve deepened it to make a helicopter fill point.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Now all this alder above us here, was that open land?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: This has been along here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, that's why I was taking photos. But above us it looked like young alder, and there was a patch right above the spring that didn't have any fir on it.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I'm not sure about that. I'm not sure that picture is . . . but my picture of Muddy Springs -- in my book -- it would show that area (maybe) above the road. It shows where the buildings are.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Lots of green out there. Thin it, log it, or whatever.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: There's one person who really wants to adopt the Giesy Plan, who really wants to turn the whole forest into a commercial carbon sink.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yes it is, I read that.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: I think I read that too.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: You know, just so you pay the children for it, so much a thousand.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Here's the thing. So many of these suggestions or proposals might bring a fair amount of money into the School Fund. They could conceivably do that. But they don't produce jobs, and we -- in the past -- we have had 400 jobs here, according to what people who are involved in listing jobs show; by jobs per million feet. So 400 jobs . . . but listen . . . carbon sinks don't produce any jobs, far as I know.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Couple of accountants.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: But, the fact is, a lot of these ivory tower figures don't care about jobs. That's not on their priority list.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, they care about jobs, that's why it's called tenure. That's a joke because it's funny but it's also absolutely true.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The one guy I was talking to that wrote the editorial though, he wanted to do jobs and carbon sink and old-growth, so divide it up into another portion. I was talking to him and I said, "Just do twenty years like we're proposing and turn the whole thing and just measure the carbon that's being sequestered, if that's. . .I don't think it's going to be so important twenty years from now as it is now, but let's say it is, they would have all the information they need on intensely managed land versus set-aside land, and we'd have the 400 jobs and 400 million dollars."

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So he seemed kind of reasonable that way compared to a lot of them, that don't want to do any cutting.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Then there's that segment, that demographic that simply is irrevocably committed to harvesting no trees. They don't care who owns them, it doesn't matter who owns them. It's “don't harvest any trees!”

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Even dead ones.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Oh absolutely. Especially dead ones, they're . . .

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Depending on what they want.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Now there's been all this “special habitat.”

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The dead ones start over again, they put carbon in the ground I guess.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well I did a paper on carbon sequestration in 1991 and then they took away my funding. That was my career with EPA, one paper.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Said something they didn't like?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I said their models couldn't work because they were too simplistic, and I think that was the nail.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They didn't want to hear that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Nope. Also that you would have to plant all the farmland in North America to compensate for the automobiles people were driving. Of course, without food they wouldn't be driving cars very long. The numbers just didn't crunch very good at that point.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This is all pure alder area, on this side over here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Pure alder?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Pure alder.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And it's been converted to fir?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Right, so that was part of our mission, to get rid of all that alder, to get fir in there at a higher value.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Now, I have to confess, at that same time, we're talking about -- of course -- all of the land. There's no such things as riparian zones, or bird set- asides; it was all of the land that you used. So today, what I've heard, is some people think that maybe 50% of the forest is manageable. Maybe half the acreage. But you know, seriously, how that works out. Again, time was when you had an easy conversion factor: for every thousand acres you can have an allowable annual cut of a million feet -- for every thousand acres. And the county, the foresters who work for the county, have six thousand acres of timberland, and they have an annual cut of six million feet. Weyerhaeuser had a hundred and thirty thousand acres and the annual allowable cut when I came to work here was a hundred, a hundred and thirty million. A year.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: A million foot in allowable cut, for a thousand acres, is pretty close to it. So they know here's the Elliott. If it's half manageable, at forty thousand acres, and that converts to forty million feet. So that whole ratio is pretty close.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: A million feet for each thousand acres. That'd be a thousand feet per acre per year, so that'd be . . .

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Depends on how much an acre is in feet. We got 4 million feet off of one 40 [acres] once, of Eliott-type timber we cut on Kentuck Inlet.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, it depends. What you got, fifty thousand feet on some of these acres out here, sixty thousand?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Something like that, but it would be something to get four million feet off of forty acres, that would be pretty good. I reckon the timbers are small.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, it'd be four . . . how many feet was it growing?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: They figured they got four million feet off of forty acres down here, that’s what they said.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So, that'd be four thousand, thousand. So . . . I used to be good at math in my head.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Probably when you weren't bumping around so much. Shaking it up a little bit.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well yeah, I think it's a sleep factor too. And an age.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, I was required to report on volume removals for every logging permit. To harvest timber you had to apply for a logging permit. Of course, they were free. And then at the end of the year -- then I had to report what area they had logged and whether they burned their slash or not, because it still was a law of the books that required burning the slash; and the volume that they reported as having harvested. entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well that went on from, see I started saving records on that in '53, and for the next 10 years they were doing normal harvesting. Then they got hit by the Columbus Day windstorm. entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But you think basically they averaged about 130 million for the 40 years?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips

So she wasn't going to defend it. Well, now see we don't know if she's a member of the Sierra Club or what her position is, and she should be doing judgments for the people of Oregon. I'm sure she would say well that's what she's doing. Just exactly what she's doing. She believes that majority people of Oregon would want that lawsuit to succeed. So go fight it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Huh.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The Governor has no background in this sort of thing at all.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well her husband was a forester, sort of.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well, yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But it's hard to tell what he did. I think he worked out of Portland and retired when she got elected.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well I want to think, or at least I try anyway, to adopt a position in my own mind that is fairly moderate. You know, I know, I realize that I'm a commodity-oriented forester. I'm a Republican, so I'm conservative, and I believe in work and jobs, and so on. I believe in those things. But, I also realize that our culture -- our culture -- has changed a lot in the last 30 or 40 years. And it's not the world I grew up in, but it is how it is today.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I have 10 grandkids who are -- well they're in their 20's and 30's -- and I will never, I think, ever find out, because I'll never know, but my guess is that they are way more liberal than I am. Five young women and five young men. But I would just believe that they probably are. They’ve gone to college at a different time than I did. And been part of our culture in this day and age. My daughter and oldest son grew up, my number two son also grew up, in Vietnam War times. And participated in protest marches, and so on. So I'm sure they're more liberal than I am. So I try hard to keep adjusting my own position on things. Otherwise, you're written off as being a hopeless case.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: And I don't want to be that.
Lakeside. 32:27 Lakeside CCC Bridge & Airport

entries.text: That wasn't Tenmile Creek, was it?

entries.text: I think they're supposed to have one of the best coho runs in the world, or used to have. And the Eel Creek, they'd have big eel runs, and Indians had

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: camping sites along them. Like a big huge deal, when they [used to fish for them].

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think that the --

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: . . . changed the lakes, that’s why --

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: . . . the original bridge back there was built by the CC's. They built the airport here, and then built that bridge. And in their monthly periodical newsletter they printed -- every camp did that -- they put a picture of that bridge in and they titled it: "The bridge that we built." They were very prideful of it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: When we started logging, we knew the CC bridge would not carry our log trucks off the state forest. So we got here with the county and we rebuilt the bridge, the one that we just drove over.
